statement: In young drivers tested in a driving simulator the morning after a night of social drinking that they chose themselves, the morning after drinking compared with the same drivers after a night without alcohol is associated with poorer driving on a short simulated commute through town and country, including in drivers with no alcohol left in their breath: in 52 drivers, eight of 15 driving measures were worse, among them slower responses to a divided-attention task (d = 0.55), more time off the road (d = 0.68), more lane excursions (d = 0.58), more centre-line crossings (d = 0.36), faster driving (d = 0.42) and more tickets for violations (d = 0.34), with similar effects in the 26 whose breath alcohol was zero, while lane-keeping variability and speed variability did not differ, and collisions differed in the analysis of variance (p = 0.04) but not in the paired comparison; in the 26 with some alcohol still in their breath, collisions also rose (d = 0.74) (Alford et al., 2020). A systematic review found that two of three earlier naturalistic driving studies reported poorer vehicle control the morning after heavy drinking and one found no change in speed; they were too different to pool (Gunn et al., 2018). Drinking amounts and sleep were not recorded and drivers knew their condition, so the effect of alcohol cannot be separated from a short night; the authors' comparison with driving at 0.05 to 0.08% blood alcohol rests on another study and was not tested in theirs, and the faster driving they attribute to residual alcohol was already present in that group on the alcohol-free morning (editors' reading). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In a driving simulator, young drivers drove worse the morning after a night out drinking than after a night without alcohol, even when a breath test showed no alcohol: they reacted more slowly, drove faster, left their lane and the road more often and got more tickets. Drivers with some alcohol still in their breath also had more crashes. Sleep was not measured, so part of the effect may come from a short night.
population: Young drivers aged 18 to 25 with 1 to 6 years of driving experience who drink socially and report regular hangovers (52 in one UK simulator study); and the participants of three earlier naturalistic driving studies summarized in a systematic review
exposure: The morning after a self-chosen night of social drinking, with breath alcohol zero (26 drivers) or still measurable (26 drivers) before driving
comparator: The same drivers on a morning after a night without alcohol
outcome: Simulated driving: divided-attention responses, vehicle control (speed, lane keeping, time off road, lane excursions, centre-line crossings) and violations (collisions, speed-limit exceedances, tickets)
magnitude: All 52 drivers, morning after drinking against alcohol-free morning (authors' Cohen's d, no intervals): divided-attention response time d = 0.55, missed responses 0.30, incorrect responses 0.21; mean speed 0.42; centre-line crossings 0.36; time off road 0.68; lane excursions 0.58; tickets 0.34; no significant difference in lane-keeping variability, speed variability, mean lane position, speed-limit exceedances or collisions. Zero breath alcohol (26): response time 0.69, speed 0.40, centre-line crossings 0.48, time off road 0.61, lane excursions 0.64. Residual breath alcohol (26): response time 0.50, speed 0.45, time off road 0.72, lane excursions 0.51, collisions 0.74. Workload rated higher after drinking (d = 0.99).

evidence.locator: Table 1, Combined Groups columns; Results › 3.1 Driving Performance, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: In all 52 drivers, eight of 15 driving measures were worse on the morning after drinking than on the morning after a night without alcohol: divided-attention response time 3.5 (SD 1.8) against 2.4 (1.3), d = 0.55; incorrect and missed responses d = 0.21 and 0.30; mean speed 35.9 against 31.7 mph, d = 0.42; centre-line crossings 7.8% against 4.0%, d = 0.36; time off road 1.6% against 0.6%, d = 0.68; lane excursions 18.9 against 10.6, d = 0.58; tickets 1.2 against 0.8, d = 0.34.

evidence.locator: Table 1, Zero BAC Group columns; Results › 3.1 Driving Performance, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: In the 26 drivers with zero breath alcohol, morning after drinking against morning after a night without alcohol: response time 3.4 against 2.3, d = 0.69; mean speed 33.7 against 29.1 mph, d = 0.40; centre-line crossings 6.0% against 3.8%, d = 0.48; time off road 1.3% against 0.5%, d = 0.61; lane excursions 20.2 against 9.7, d = 0.64; collisions 1.1 against 1.6, not significant.

evidence.locator: Table 1, Lane Deviation, Speed Deviation, Mean Lane Position, Accidents and Collisions and Speed Limit Exceedances rows; Results › 3.1, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Introduction, 2nd paragraph; 2.4 Driving Simulator Test, last paragraph
evidence.extracted: Lane deviation (2.9 against 2.6), speed variability, mean lane position and speed-limit exceedances did not differ significantly between the two mornings in all 52 drivers; for collisions (1.8 against 1.3) the ANOVA alcohol effect was significant (p = 0.04) but the paired comparison was not. Lane deviation appears to be the SDLP listed in the Methods, the principal measure of the 'gold standard' highway test.

evidence.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 (Residual Alcohol Group); Results › 3.1
evidence.locator: Table 1, Control and Hangover columns of the Zero BAC and Residual Alcohol groups; Results › 3.1 Driving Performance, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Drivers with residual breath alcohol had more collisions on the morning after drinking than on their alcohol-free morning (2.5 against 0.9, d = 0.74), the only driving measure with an alcohol-by-group interaction. The authors attribute the residual group's faster driving, more speed-limit exceedances and more tickets to residual alcohol, but that group also drove faster, exceeded limits more and got more tickets on the alcohol-free morning (34.3 against 29.1 mph; 10.4 against 7.0 exceedances; 1.0 against 0.6 tickets), so these group differences cannot be attributed to residual alcohol (editors' note).

Drinking was unobserved and amounts are not reported (some participants could not recall them); sleep was not recorded, and the authors note that sleep loss may be a significant component of hangover effects on next-day performance. Their statement that the impairment is equivalent to driving at or above 0.05-0.08% blood alcohol cites another study's simulated highway test (ref 21); no alcohol benchmark was run in this study.

Of three naturalistic studies of driving the morning after heavy drinking, two found poorer control of the vehicle (deviation from a set course; Laurell and Törnros, 1983; Verster et al., 2014) and one found no next-day effect on speed (Törnros and Laurell, 1991); differences in method prevented pooling.

risk_of_bias.note: Naturalistic within-person comparison: drinking nights self-chosen, amounts and sleep unrecorded, drivers and experimenters aware of condition, three unregistered studies combined; the earlier studies are seen only through a review and cannot be appraised here.

inconsistency.note: The direction is consistent across studies, but the measures differ: weaving increased on a long highway drive in one earlier study, while on this short urban route weaving did not change and lane excursions and time off road did.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for simulated driving in young drivers, as studied; real-road crash risk is not claimed.

imprecision.note: No intervals are reported; with 52 drivers in a within-person design, effects of the reported size are unlikely to be chance, but the size is uncertain.

grade.reasoning: Observational within-person evidence starts low and is downgraded once for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated: poorer vehicle control the morning after drinking was reported by this study and by at least one independent earlier group (Laurell and Törnros, 1983), with Verster et al. (2014) sharing an author with Alford et al.; only this study separated drivers with zero from those with residual breath alcohol. The claim does not repeat the authors' equivalence with a legal blood alcohol limit or their residual-alcohol speeding finding, which the data do not support.
